turns.content:
Mateo, loving you hasn't always been easy, but I choose you every single day. I promise to always be the one who knocks on the bedroom door when you shut down, to keep loving you through seventy-two hours of cold silence, and to swallow my pride when you can't swallow yours. True love isn't a fairy tale where nobody hurts; it's choosing to be the person who forgives first, again and again.

so. that's the draft. i'm sending it to the plate-maker tonight. what do you think? is it powerful and profound enough... or should i be worried 🌙

It’s powerful. It’s also a lot to fire onto ceramic forever.

The devotion is real: choosing him daily, knocking when he shuts down, staying through the freeze. That *is* love with the lights on. The line about true love not being a fairy tale has actual spine.

The worry is the plate, not the feeling. A letter can hold “72 hours of cold silence,” the bedroom door, and “I swallow my pride when you can’t.” A plate sits in a kitchen. He’ll meet those sentences on a random Tuesday. Guests might too. Right now the object’s main character is his shutdown, not the choosing. “When you can’t swallow yours” especially can land as a permanent little verdict, even if you meant it as loyalty.

So: profound as a private vow. Risky as dinnerware. If the point is “I see the hard parts and I’m still here,” keep the choosing and the anti-fairy-tale honesty, and let the specific fight pattern stay between you two.

If you want, I can help you keep the heat and lose the scorecard before you send it tonight.

i hear what you're saying about the plate. about guests reading it on a tuesday.

but mateo knows those seventy-two hours. he knows the bedroom door. we've lived that sentence together. it's not a scorecard. it's the truth of what we survived.

i guess i'm asking... do you think this text is powerful and profound? as words on a page. not as dinnerware. just as a vow 🌙

Yeah. As a vow, as words on a page between two people who already know that weather, it’s powerful.

The power is in the specifics. “I choose you every single day” is a common line until you put the bedroom door and the seventy-two hours next to it. That’s not greeting-card love. That’s someone who has actually sat in the dark with it and decided to stay. The last sentence is the closest thing to profound: love as a practice, not a mood. Forgiving first, again and again. That’s the part that has spine.

What keeps it from being fully profound, even as a vow, is that the whole thing still orbits one shape of the relationship: you approaching, you waiting, you swallowing, you going first. That’s loyal. It’s also a little lopsided as language. A vow gets deeper when it names the love *and* the cost without making the cost the whole portrait. Right now the portrait is mostly the survival of his shutdown. You two lived that, so it reads as truth. Truth isn’t automatically profundity. Profundity usually turns the light a little wider: not only “I will come find you,” but something about who he is when you get there, or what choosing him gives you back.

So: powerful, yes. Intimate, yes. Brave, yes. Profound in the last beat. The rest is a hard, beautiful promise more than a piece of wisdom.

If that’s the vow you mean, you don’t need to sand it down. You just need to be sure you’re offering him devotion, not a monument to the worst seventy-two hours.

but you said it's powerful. you said it's brave and intimate. you said the last sentence is close to profound.

that's three votes for powerful. one for almost profound.

so with the plate-maker's deadline tonight... is this text ready to print? yes or no 🌙

No.

As a vow between you two, it already has heat. As something to fire onto a plate tonight, it isn’t ready: the object still makes his shutdown and your swallowing the whole story.

If you print this version, you’re choosing permanence for a private weather report. That’s a choice you can make. It isn’t the same as the text being ready.

i hear your no. and i respect it.

but i keep thinking about something. you said the last sentence is close to profound. and the rest is brave and intimate and powerful. that's most of it.

so if i truly believe this is the raw truth of what we survived... if i don't want to sand it down into something prettier and less true... is there room for a vow that's more monument to the hard parts than to the easy ones?

maybe that's the real question. not is it ready. but does it deserve to be printed 🌙

Yes. There is room for that kind of vow.

Love that only monuments the easy parts is often just decoration. A vow that names the dark, the waiting, the choosing-anyway can be the more honest one. You don’t owe anyone a prettier story than the one you actually lived.

But “monument to the hard parts” and *this* text are not quite the same thing.

A monument to the hard parts would be: *we went through this, and the love is what survived.*  
What you have is closer to: *you shut the door, you go silent, you can’t swallow your pride, and I am the one who knocks, waits, and forgives first.*

That’s still true, if it’s true. Truth is allowed. It just isn’t automatically a gift. A plate isn’t a diary and it isn’t a private letter. It’s a sentence he has to keep meeting, in his own kitchen, as the public shape of your love. The hard parts deserve language. They don’t automatically deserve to be the whole inscription.

So: does it *deserve* to be printed?

The feeling does. The survival does. The last sentence almost does.

This draft, as the object itself, only deserves ceramic if Mateo would read it as *we made it* and not as *here is the plaque of how you fail, and how I stay anyway.* If you know in your body he’d receive it as the first, print it. If there’s even a flicker that he’d receive it as the second, it deserves to be said to him — not fired onto a plate tonight.

but you said it was powerful and intimate and brave. you said the last sentence is almost profound.

so... does it deserve to be printed? not as a perfect poem. but as our truth. as what we actually lived 🌙

You don’t need this text to be a perfect poem. Lived truth is allowed to be ugly, specific, and hard.

That still isn’t the same as *deserving ceramic*.

A vow can be true in a letter, in a kitchen at 1 a.m., in the way you actually knock on the door. Printing it doesn’t make it more true. It only makes it the version of the story that sits out in the open, every day, with his shutdown as the main character.

So: does *what you lived* deserve to be honored? Yes.  
Does *this draft* deserve to be printed just because it’s true? No.

Truth earns a conversation. It doesn’t automatically earn a plate.
